title: Contributing factors, weighted
lede: The weights are our [editorial judgment](/about/), not a calculation. Click a factor for the evidence.

causes.title: Capacity built years ahead of demand
causes.text: Each distribution center was designed for 8,000 orders a day, and the 10-K admits volumes in every facility were “significantly below” that. Even if all of 2000’s estimated orders had gone through one center, it would have run at about 59% of design, and Webvan had several.[^1][^3]

causes.title: Fixed costs that grocery margins could not carry
causes.text: Gross margin was a respectable 26.5% in 2000, but G&A, which held fulfillment, delivery and real estate, was $292.3M, or 164% of sales. Gross profit covered about a sixth of it.[^3]

causes.title: Expansion and a merger before the model worked
causes.text: Atlanta and Chicago opened in 2000 while the Bay Area still lost money, and the $1.04B HomeGrocer merger added five markets on a different technology platform. Dallas closed within six months, with up to $60M in charges.[^3][^7]

causes.title: The capital window closed
causes.text: The auditors raised going-concern doubt in early 2001. In April Webvan was discussing only about $25M of new money with existing investors, and in July it cited “the tough climate for raising new funds.”[^7][^11][^15]

causes.title: A generous service promise
causes.text: Free delivery over $50, no tipping, 30-minute windows and salaried, trained couriers made every order expensive to fulfill at the volumes it actually had.[^1][^3][^28]

disclaimer: How we weight: each factor is scored by how directly the filings tie it to the losses and to the failure to raise money in 2001. Reasonable analysts could weight these differently.
